title: Take the planner's overrides, and name the ones that clash

expected.says: Run's report for the tiny season matches the expected report

blueprint.signature: def build(season: Season, overrides: tuple[Override, ...] = ()) -> TrimModel
blueprint.contract: The model of the lesson before, moved to model.py with crew_ids, horizon and start_domain, and built with the overrides. Every rule a planner can change sits behind a named literal, with its words: `must_<cid>` (`<cid> is overdue and must be trimmed this season`), budget (`the season's budget is $<budget>k`, the budget written with a thousands comma, as f"{budget:,}" writes it: `$962k`, `$1,000k`) and `override_<i>` (`override <i>: ` followed by the override's own words, as Override.says gives them: `trim <cid> on <crew> from week <start> (<reason>)` for a pin, `leave <cid> for next season (<reason>)`, `trim <cid> this season (<reason>)`, with `no reason given` when the reason is empty). A skip leaves its circuit untrimmed; a pin or force trims it; a pin also fixes the crew and the first week it names. The rules are made in this order: each must as its circuit comes in the season's order, then the budget, then the overrides in the order given.
blueprint.idea: A rule behind a literal holds only when its literal is true, so the search can be asked which literals cannot all be true.

blueprint.signature: def holds(tm: TrimModel, names: list[str]) -> bool
blueprint.contract: Answers whether the named rules can all hold at once: clears the model's assumptions, adds the named rules' literals as assumptions, and solves with num_workers = 1 and stop_after_first_solution = True; True unless the status is INFEASIBLE.
blueprint.idea: Only yes or no matters, so the first plan found is enough.

blueprint.contract: Returns a minimal list of rule names that cannot all hold, or [] when every rule can: the rules the solver names as sufficient for infeasibility (assumptions need one worker), then each dropped in turn and left out when the rest still cannot hold. The names come back in the order the rules were made, whatever order the solver named them in.
blueprint.idea: Assumptions name a set of rules that is enough for the proof; a deletion filter makes it minimal.

lesson.title: 9.1.5 CP-SAT Assumptions as a Conflict Finder

blueprint.signature: def why_infeasible(season: Season, overrides: tuple[Override, ...] = ()) -> list[str]
blueprint.contract: Builds the model of the season and its overrides and returns the words (TrimModel.says) of the rules in its conflict, in the conflict's order. The tests compare the explanation with an exact tuple in that order: musts, then the budget, then the overrides.
blueprint.idea: A conflict is only useful in the words of the people who can change it.

lesson.title: 9.1.6 Turning an IIS Into a Planner Message

blueprint.signature: def check_overrides(season: Season, overrides: tuple[Override, ...]) -> list[str]
blueprint.contract: Returns what is wrong with the overrides as data, in order: `override <i>: unknown kind <kind repr>` unless the kind is pin, skip or force; `override <i>: no circuit <cid>`; `override <i>: no crew <crew>`; `override <i>: week <start> is outside the season`. Empty when nothing is.
blueprint.idea: An override that names nothing is refused before any model is built.

lesson.title: 12.1.2 Manual Overrides as Bounds, With an Audit Trail

blueprint.signature: def make_plan(season: Season, overrides: tuple[Override, ...] = ()) -> Plan
blueprint.contract: Raises ValueError with the problems joined by `; ` when check_overrides finds any; otherwise solves with every rule's literal true, and when the season is INFEASIBLE returns a Plan whose explanation is why_infeasible's words.
blueprint.idea: A failed plan says which of the planner's rules clash, not just that it failed.

lesson.title: 14.1.6 Planner Overrides and Why a Plan Failed

blueprint.signature: def format_plan(season: Season, plan: Plan) -> str
blueprint.contract: After the crews, when the plan has an explanation, the line `these rules cannot all hold; change one of them:` and one line `  - <words>` per rule, in the explanation's order. An INFEASIBLE plan has no trims, so its status line reads `0 trims, cost $0k, risk carried $0k` and each crew's line shows only its weeks off, ending in two spaces.
blueprint.idea: The explanation is part of the answer, so the report prints it.
